conceptTag: How a small grocer competes with a giant
readerTitle: The supermarket opened down the road. Now what?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 식료품점, 가정 청소 업체) · 집중 전략과 어중간함의 함정을 적용
insight: 거대 경쟁자와 맞설 때는 '어디서 이길까'보다 '그들이 잘 못 챙기는 고객은 누구인가'를 먼저 묻는다.
misconception: 큰 경쟁자가 오면 가격을 맞추고 품목을 늘려야 손님을 지킬 수 있다.

sources.text: Porter, M. (1980). Competitive Strategy. Free Press. (집중 전략, 어중간함의 함정)
모든 사례와 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례는 설명용 가상 사례이며 구체적 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다. '대형 업체가 구매력으로 더 싸게 산다'는 일반론으로만 서술했습니다.
7번 카드의 '대형 체인이 소형 매장 형태로 동네에 들어온다'는 일반적으로 관찰되는 흐름으로만 적었고 특정 기업을 언급하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The supermarket opened down the road. Now what?
body: Maria has run a small grocery on a busy city street for twelve years. Last month, a huge supermarket opened two kilometres away.
It has ten times her range and lower prices on almost everything. Her first instinct is to fight it on its own terms. That instinct is worth a second look.

image.label: A tiny corner shop facing a giant supermarket
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 아늑한 작은 동네 식료품점(차양, 과일 진열대), 오른쪽 멀리 거대한 창고형 슈퍼마켓과 넓은 주차장. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상호는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Maria do first?
body: Sales are down. She has a little cash saved and one chance to make a real change.

options.text: Cut prices on her 50 best-sellers to match the supermarket
options.feedback: She gives up margin on a fight she can't win. The giant buys in bulk and can go lower for longer. **Cost leadership** belongs to whoever has the lowest costs, and that isn't her.

options.text: Find the customers the supermarket serves badly and build around them
options.feedback: This is **focus**: serve a narrow group better than a broad rival can. She stops competing for everyone and starts winning someone.

options.text: Stock more products so customers never need to go elsewhere
options.feedback: Range helps a little, but she'll never out-stock a supermarket. More shelves mean more cost and more waste, with no clear reason to pick her.

cards.title: Not everyone left.
body: Maria spent a week watching who still came in. Three groups stood out: older neighbours who walk, people from the new apartment blocks nearby, and shift workers buying dinner at 9 p.m.
None of them wanted a weekly car trip. They wanted something close, quick and open late.
The supermarket is built for the big Saturday shop. Her remaining customers were buying something different: **tonight's dinner, without the drive**.

cards.title: Focus: be the best choice for a few
body: A focused business picks a narrow group and shapes everything around what that group needs. A broad rival can't do the same without bending its whole model.
The supermarket could stay open until midnight, but a huge store with a skeleton crew costs a lot to run. It could sell dinner kits, but they'd sit among thousands of other products.
Maria's size is a weakness on price. For this group, it's a strength.

image.label: One big circle of all shoppers, one small highlighted circle
image.brief: 큰 원 안에 다양한 쇼핑객 아이콘(자동차로 장보는 가족 등). 그 안의 작은 원에 걸어오는 노인, 아파트 주민, 밤 근무자 아이콘을 밝게 강조. 작은 원 옆에 작은 가게 아이콘.

cards.title: Where should the money go?
body: Maria has budget for one main change. Which fits her focus best?

options.text: Open until 11 p.m., sell ready-to-cook dinner kits, deliver to the apartment blocks
options.feedback: Each choice serves the same customers and supports the others. Late hours bring shift workers, kits sell the evening meal, delivery reaches walkers. This is **focus** done fully.

options.text: A loyalty card with discounts on weekly staples
options.feedback: It keeps some regulars, but it rewards the weekly shop, which is the supermarket's home ground. She'd pay for loyalty without changing why people choose her.

options.text: A bit cheaper, a bit more premium, a bit more range
options.feedback: This is the path to being **stuck in the middle**: not cheapest, not special, not convenient. Every change costs money, and none gives a clear reason to come.

cards.title: A little of everything wins no one.
body: Option C feels safe because it spreads the risk. In practice, it spreads the money too thin.

A business that is **stuck in the middle** has higher costs than the low-price leader and less appeal than the specialist. Customers who want cheap go to the giant. Customers who want convenience find someone more convenient.
Maria's real choice was not *how much* to change. It was *for whom*.

cards.title: Focus has conditions.
body: The group must be big enough to pay the bills. Three loyal neighbours can't cover rent.
It must also be hard for the giant to serve. If big chains open small, late-night stores nearby, the gap closes. A focused business has to keep checking that its niche still exists.
And focus means saying no. Some customers will leave, and that has to be all right.
cards.softwareNote: A small software company facing a giant platform often wins the same way: serving one industry's workflow deeply, such as scheduling for dental clinics, where the big general tool feels clumsy.

cards.title: Now it's a home cleaning business.
body: You run a five-person cleaning team. A national chain arrives with an app, instant booking and lower prices. Your clients include many elderly homeowners and families with pets.

options.text: Build your own booking app and cut prices 15%
options.feedback: You'd spend heavily to copy the chain's strengths and still lose on cost. This drifts toward **stuck in the middle**.

options.text: Specialise in pet homes and older clients: same trusted cleaner each visit, a phone call to book
options.feedback: **Focus**. The chain's rotating staff and app-first booking suit these clients poorly. Your consistency is hard for them to match at scale.

options.text: Keep everything the same and wait for clients to tire of the chain
options.feedback: Some will return, but without a clear reason to choose you, the drift continues.

cards.softwareNote: The chain's app is its strength with busy younger clients. For clients who prefer a phone call and a familiar face, it is friction.

cards.title: Don't fight the giant everywhere. Win where it's clumsy.
body: **Concepts used:** *Focus* (serve a narrow group better than a broad rival can) and *Stuck in the middle* (a little of everything wins no one).
**Try it today:** list your three most loyal customer types. For each, write one thing a bigger rival does badly for them.
